titleStmt.author: Andrew M. Guess
Jonathan Nagler

bibl.title: Less than you think: Prevalence and predictors of fake news dissemination on Facebook

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: who actually posted links from fake news domains to their Facebook friends during the 2016 US campaign, measured from profile data rather than from what people say they did
span.quote: Our approach allows us to provide a comprehensive observational portrait of the individual-level characteristics related to posting articles from fake news–spreading domains to friends on social media.

span.label: how common fake news sharing was, and which individual characteristics predict it once ideology, partisanship, education and overall posting volume are held constant
span.quote: We link a representative online survey (N = 3500) to behavioral data on respondents’ Facebook sharing history during the campaign, avoiding known biases in self-reports of online activity.

span.label: a survey of 3500 linked to 1191 respondents' real Facebook sharing: over 90% shared no fake news at all, conservatives shared more, and the oldest group shared nearly seven times as much as the youngest with everything else held constant
span.quote: So-called “fake news” has renewed concerns about the prevalence and effects of misinformation in political campaigns. Given the potential for widespread dissemination of this material, we examine the individual-level characteristics associated with sharing false articles during the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign. To do so, we uniquely link an original survey with respondents’ sharing activity as recorded in Facebook profile data. First and foremost, we find that sharing this content was a relatively rare activity. Conservatives were more likely to share articles from fake news domains, which in 2016 were largely pro-Trump in orientation, than liberals or moderates. We also find a strong age effect, which persists after controlling for partisanship and ideology: On average, users over 65 shared nearly seven times as many articles from fake news domains as the youngest age group.

span.label: existence
span.quote: So-called “fake news” has renewed concerns about the prevalence and effects of misinformation in political campaigns. Given the potential for widespread dissemination of this material, we examine the individual-level characteristics associated with sharing false articles during the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign. To do so, we uniquely link an original survey with respondents’ sharing activity as recorded in Facebook profile data. First and foremost, we find that sharing this content was a relatively rare activity. Conservatives were more likely to share articles from fake news domains, which in 2016 were largely pro-Trump in orientation, than liberals or moderates. We also find a strong age effect, which persists after controlling for partisanship and ideology: On average, users over 65 shared nearly seven times as many articles from fake news domains as the youngest age group.

span.label: the dissemination of deliberately false political content by ordinary users - rare, concentrated, and predicted by age more robustly than by anything else measured
span.quote: More puzzling is the independent role of age: Holding constant ideology, party identification, or both, respondents in each age category were more likely to share fake news than respondents in the next-youngest group, and the gap in the rate of fake news sharing between those in our oldest category (over 65) and youngest category is large and notable.

span.label: a three-wave YouGov panel linked by consent to Facebook timeline data, with posted domains cross-referenced against journalist- and academic-built lists of fake news publishers, modelled as counts by quasi-Poisson regression with sample-matching weights
span.term: a three-wave YouGov panel linked by consent to Facebook timeline data, with posted domains cross-referenced against journalist- and academic-built lists of fake news publishers, modelled as counts by quasi-Poisson regression with sample-matching weights
span.quote: We aggregated all shares to the individual respondent level so that our dependent variables are counts (i.e., number of fake news stories shared). To account for this feature of the data, as well as the highly skewed distribution of the counts, we primarily used Poisson or quasi-Poisson regressions to model the determinants of Facebook sharing behavior. We conducted dispersion tests on the count data and used quasi-Poisson models if the null hypothesis of no dispersion is rejected. Below, we included negative binomial and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions to show that our results are generally not sensitive to model choice.

span.label: BuzzSumo ranks domains by Facebook engagement; a journalist checks each for the hallmark features of a fake news site - no contact page, syndicated content, recently registered; a supervised classifier trained on 7 million pages removes anything it calls hard news. Thirty domains become twenty-one, and every share in the dependent variable is a link to one of those twenty-one
span.term: a category built by three procedures in sequence
span.quote: Our BuzzFeed-based list began with 30 domains identified by that site’s reporting as purveyors of intentionally false election-related stories generating the most Facebook engagement. To do this, the journalists, led by Craig Silverman, used keywords and existing lists combined with the analytics service BuzzSumo. To ensure that our analysis stayed clear of websites that could be construed as partisan or hyperpartisan (rather than intentionally or systematically factually inaccurate), we additionally filtered out domains identified as hard news by a supervised learning classifier developed by Bakshy et al.. The nearly 500 hard news domains encompass a wide range of news and opinion websites, both mainstream and niche. The classifier was trained on the text features of roughly 7 million web pages shared on Facebook over a 6-month period by U.S. users, with training labels for hard and soft news generated using bootstrapped keyword searches on the URLs.

span.label: linking profile data to a survey removes the self-report bias in what people say they shared, and it cannot recover what they thought they were sharing. The design buys accuracy about the act and gives up access to the state of mind - which is the quantity the survey experiments measure and cannot observe the act of
span.quote: Figure 2D shows that, if anything, those who share the most content in general were less likely to share articles from fake news–spreading domains to their friends. Thus, it is not the case that what explains fake news sharing is simply that some respondents “will share anything.” These data are consistent with the hypothesis that people who share many links are more familiar with what they are seeing and are able to distinguish fake news from real news. (We note that we have no measure as to whether or not respondents know that what they are sharing is fake news.)

span.label: 3500 respondents, 1331 consenting to share profile data, 1191 successfully linked - and the linked respondents were more knowledgeable and more politically engaged than those who declined. The behavioural half of the design is available only from people willing to hand it over, and willingness correlates with the subject matter
span.term: a consent gradient inside the sample
span.quote: Of 3500 initial respondents in wave 1, 1331 (38%) agreed to share Facebook profile data with us. The proportion rises (49.1%) when we consider that only 2711 of our respondents said that they use Facebook at all. We were successfully able to link profile data from 1191 of survey respondents, leaving us with approximately 44% of Facebook users in our sample. (See the “Sample details” section for a comparison of sample characteristics on various demographic and behavioral dimensions. Linked respondents were somewhat more knowledgeable and engaged in politics than those who did not share data.)

span.label: sharing is a choice made over what arrived. Without the News Feed, a group that shares more fake news may be a group that saw more of it, and no amount of control for the sharer's characteristics separates the two. The authors state this rather than resolving it
span.term: the unobserved half of every social media finding
span.quote: In addition, while our approach allows for enhanced measurement of online sharing behavior, we lack data on the composition of respondents’ Facebook News Feeds. It is possible, for instance, that very conservative Facebook users were exposed to more fake news articles in their networks and that the patterns we observe are not due to differential willingness to believe or share false content across the political spectrum. While other evidence suggests the limits of the “echo chambers” narrative, we cannot rule out this possibility.

span.label: there is no measure of whether respondents knew that what they shared was false
span.quote: Figure 2D shows that, if anything, those who share the most content in general were less likely to share articles from fake news–spreading domains to their friends. Thus, it is not the case that what explains fake news sharing is simply that some respondents “will share anything.” These data are consistent with the hypothesis that people who share many links are more familiar with what they are seeing and are able to distinguish fake news from real news. (We note that we have no measure as to whether or not respondents know that what they are sharing is fake news.)

span.label: the data are observational and cannot provide causal evidence, and an omitted variable cannot be definitively ruled out
span.quote: We cannot definitively rule out the possibility that there is an omitted variable biasing our estimates, although we have included controls for many individual-level characteristics theoretically related to acceptance of misinformation and willingness to share content online. Even if our models are correctly specified, we use observational data that cannot provide causal evidence on the determinants of fake news sharing.

span.label: half the respondents with Facebook accounts declined to share their profile data, and the linked ones were more knowledgeable and politically engaged
span.quote: However, we are still limited in our ability to collect these data unobtrusively. Despite our high response rate, half of our respondents with Facebook accounts opted not to share their profile data with us. Any inferences are therefore limited insofar as the likelihood of sharing data is correlated with other characteristics of interest.

span.label: the composition of respondents' News Feeds is unobserved, so exposure cannot be separated from willingness to share
span.quote: In addition, while our approach allows for enhanced measurement of online sharing behavior, we lack data on the composition of respondents’ Facebook News Feeds. It is possible, for instance, that very conservative Facebook users were exposed to more fake news articles in their networks and that the patterns we observe are not due to differential willingness to believe or share false content across the political spectrum. While other evidence suggests the limits of the “echo chambers” narrative, we cannot rule out this possibility.

span.label: posts deleted before consent are invisible, and the authors argue rather than measure that this should reduce noise rather than bias
span.quote: There may be an additional concern that some types of people were more likely to delete fake news articles that they posted, leading us to biased inferences. However, to the extent that these characteristics are negatively correlated with the characteristics that predict posting in the first place, such deletion activity (which is likely very rare) should reduce noise in the data that would otherwise be generated by split-second sharing decisions that are immediately retracted.

span.label: the conservative finding is sensitive to coding and rests on a small number of respondents
span.quote: We find some evidence that the most conservative users were more likely to share this content—the vast majority of which was pro-Trump in orientation—than were other Facebook users, although this is sensitive to coding and based on a small number of respondents.

span.label: the ideological pattern may reflect the pro-Trump slant of the available content and the ordinary tendency to share what one agrees with, rather than a greater propensity to share falsehood
span.quote: This is consistent with the pro-Trump slant of most fake news articles produced during the 2016 campaign, and of the tendency of respondents to share articles they agree with, and thus might not represent a greater tendency of conservatives to share fake news than liberals conditional on being exposed to it.

span.label: there is no commonly accepted ground-truth standard for what counts as fake news, so the dependent variable rests on lists built by journalists and academics
span.quote: The term fake news can be used to refer to a variety of different phenomena. Here, we largely adopted the use suggested in of knowingly false or misleading content created largely for the purpose of generating ad revenue. Given the difficulty of establishing a commonly accepted ground-truth standard for what constitutes fake news, our approach was to build on the work of both journalists and academics who worked to document the prevalence of this content over the course of the 2016 election campaign.

span.label: digital trace data linked to survey response, carried from computational social science into a question political science had been answering with self-report
span.quote: We link a representative online survey (N = 3500) to behavioral data on respondents’ Facebook sharing history during the campaign, avoiding known biases in self-reports of online activity.

span.label: a supervised text classifier from information retrieval, used not to make the finding but to draw the boundary of the outcome variable
span.quote: Our BuzzFeed-based list began with 30 domains identified by that site’s reporting as purveyors of intentionally false election-related stories generating the most Facebook engagement. To do this, the journalists, led by Craig Silverman, used keywords and existing lists combined with the analytics service BuzzSumo. To ensure that our analysis stayed clear of websites that could be construed as partisan or hyperpartisan (rather than intentionally or systematically factually inaccurate), we additionally filtered out domains identified as hard news by a supervised learning classifier developed by Bakshy et al.. The nearly 500 hard news domains encompass a wide range of news and opinion websites, both mainstream and niche. The classifier was trained on the text features of roughly 7 million web pages shared on Facebook over a 6-month period by U.S. users, with training labels for hard and soft news generated using bootstrapped keyword searches on the URLs.

span.label: the total number of links shared of any kind reported beside the fake news count, and included as a covariate in every model
span.note: eliminates: a low fake-news count meaning people do not share links - most respondents shared hundreds, so the rarity is about the content · outcome: held
span.quote: It is important to be clear about how rare this behavior is on social platforms: The vast majority of Facebook users in our data did not share any articles from fake news domains in 2016 at all (Fig. 1), and as the left panel shows, this is not because people generally do not share links: While 3.4% of respondents for whom we have Facebook profile data shared 10 or fewer links of any kind, 310 (26.1%) respondents shared 10 to 100 links during the period of data collection and 729 (61.3%) respondents shared 100 to 1000 links.

span.label: the relationship between overall sharing volume and fake news sharing examined directly, rather than only controlled for
span.note: eliminates: the explanation that some respondents will share anything - the heaviest sharers shared LESS fake news, which is the opposite of that prediction · outcome: held
span.quote: Figure 2D shows that, if anything, those who share the most content in general were less likely to share articles from fake news–spreading domains to their friends. Thus, it is not the case that what explains fake news sharing is simply that some respondents “will share anything.” These data are consistent with the hypothesis that people who share many links are more familiar with what they are seeing and are able to distinguish fake news from real news. (We note that we have no measure as to whether or not respondents know that what they are sharing is fake news.)

span.label: the same model applied to hard news sharing as a placebo outcome
span.note: eliminates: age predicting online sharing in general - if it did, the predictors of hard news would look the same, and they do not include age at all · outcome: held
span.quote: Last, we show in table S14 that, when we try to explain patterns of hard news sharing behavior using the same approach, the predictors are more varied and do not include age.

span.label: five different lists of fake news domains, including one built from 948 individual fact-checks and one crowdsourced, with the analysis rerun on each
span.note: eliminates: one journalist's list carrying the finding - the category has no ground truth, so the robustness has to be to the choice of vocabulary itself · outcome: held
span.quote: In addition to these primary measures, we report (below) analyses using three supplementary collections of fake news articles produced after the election. Two lists were also produced by Silverman and his team at BuzzFeed, and the third is a crowdsourced effort headed by Melissa Zimdars of Merrimack College. Our key results are essentially invariant to whatever measure of fake news we use.

span.label: an exact-URL variant of the analysis using only the 948 fact-checked stories, rather than counting every article from a listed domain
span.note: eliminates: the assumption that everything published by a fake news domain is fake - the stricter definition does not need it · outcome: held
span.quote: The Allcott and Gentzkow list begins with 948 fact checks of false stories from the campaign. We retrieved the domains of the publishers originating the claims and again removed all hard news domains as described above. Then, we coded any article from this set of domains as a fake news article. For robustness, in table S9, we used only exact URL matches to any of the 948 entries in the Allcott and Gentzkow list as a more restrictive definition of fake news, but one that does not require assuming that every article from a “fake news domain” should be coded as fake news.

span.label: hard news domains removed from the list by a classifier trained on 7 million shared pages, so that hyperpartisan sites are excluded from the outcome
span.note: eliminates: the contested hyperpartisan category being counted as fake news, which would make an ideological finding partly definitional · outcome: held
span.quote: We took this list and removed all domains classified as “hard news” via the supervised learning technique used by Bakshy et al. to focus specifically on fake news domains rather than the more contested category of “hyperpartisan” sites (such as Breitbart).

span.label: negative binomial and OLS models run alongside the quasi-Poisson, with the quasi-Poisson chosen by a dispersion test
span.note: eliminates: the count model's distributional assumptions producing the result · outcome: held
span.quote: We aggregated all shares to the individual respondent level so that our dependent variables are counts (i.e., number of fake news stories shared). To account for this feature of the data, as well as the highly skewed distribution of the counts, we primarily used Poisson or quasi-Poisson regressions to model the determinants of Facebook sharing behavior. We conducted dispersion tests on the count data and used quasi-Poisson models if the null hypothesis of no dispersion is rejected. Below, we included negative binomial and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions to show that our results are generally not sensitive to model choice.

span.label: ideology and party identification, correlated at r = 0.31, entered separately and together, with all three specifications reported
span.note: eliminates: a collinearity decision being made silently in the authors' favour - they name the correlation and publish every version · outcome: held
span.quote: In all models, we included either five-point ideological self-placement, three-point party identification, or both. Since these variables were correlated (r = 0.31), we addressed possible multicollinearity via transparency—we provided our main results all three ways.

span.label: the models re-fitted as negative binomial and OLS alongside the Poisson and quasi-Poisson specifications, with dispersion tests deciding between the latter two
span.note: eliminates: that the sharing result is an artefact of one count-model specification · outcome: held

span.label: respondents asked to check which categories of profile information they were willing to share, with no access to News Feeds or to friends' data
span.note: eliminates: collecting more than was consented to - the field-by-field opt-in bounds the data at the point of collection · outcome: held
span.quote: Those who consented to do so were asked to provide access to a Facebook web application and to specifically check which types of information they were willing to share with us: fields from their public profile, including religious and political views; their own timeline posts, including external links; and “likes” of pages. We did not have access to the content of people’s News Feeds or information about their friends.

span.label: fake news
span.quote: The term fake news can be used to refer to a variety of different phenomena. Here, we largely adopted the use suggested in of knowingly false or misleading content created largely for the purpose of generating ad revenue. Given the difficulty of establishing a commonly accepted ground-truth standard for what constitutes fake news, our approach was to build on the work of both journalists and academics who worked to document the prevalence of this content over the course of the 2016 election campaign.

span.label: hard news
span.quote: We took this list and removed all domains classified as “hard news” via the supervised learning technique used by Bakshy et al. to focus specifically on fake news domains rather than the more contested category of “hyperpartisan” sites (such as Breitbart).

span.label: links
span.quote: It is important to be clear about how rare this behavior is on social platforms: The vast majority of Facebook users in our data did not share any articles from fake news domains in 2016 at all (Fig. 1), and as the left panel shows, this is not because people generally do not share links: While 3.4% of respondents for whom we have Facebook profile data shared 10 or fewer links of any kind, 310 (26.1%) respondents shared 10 to 100 links during the period of data collection and 729 (61.3%) respondents shared 100 to 1000 links.

span.label: age
span.quote: More puzzling is the independent role of age: Holding constant ideology, party identification, or both, respondents in each age category were more likely to share fake news than respondents in the next-youngest group, and the gap in the rate of fake news sharing between those in our oldest category (over 65) and youngest category is large and notable.

span.label: ideology
span.quote: More puzzling is the independent role of age: Holding constant ideology, party identification, or both, respondents in each age category were more likely to share fake news than respondents in the next-youngest group, and the gap in the rate of fake news sharing between those in our oldest category (over 65) and youngest category is large and notable.

span.label: News Feeds
span.quote: In addition, while our approach allows for enhanced measurement of online sharing behavior, we lack data on the composition of respondents’ Facebook News Feeds. It is possible, for instance, that very conservative Facebook users were exposed to more fake news articles in their networks and that the patterns we observe are not due to differential willingness to believe or share false content across the political spectrum. While other evidence suggests the limits of the “echo chambers” narrative, we cannot rule out this possibility.

span.label: quasi-Poisson
span.quote: We aggregated all shares to the individual respondent level so that our dependent variables are counts (i.e., number of fake news stories shared). To account for this feature of the data, as well as the highly skewed distribution of the counts, we primarily used Poisson or quasi-Poisson regressions to model the determinants of Facebook sharing behavior. We conducted dispersion tests on the count data and used quasi-Poisson models if the null hypothesis of no dispersion is rejected. Below, we included negative binomial and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions to show that our results are generally not sensitive to model choice.

span.label: digital media literacy
span.quote: Two potential explanations warrant further investigation. First, following research in sociology and media studies, it is possible that an entire cohort of Americans, now in their 60s and beyond, lacks the level of digital media literacy necessary to reliably determine the trustworthiness of news encountered online. There is a well-established research literature on media literacy and its importance for navigating new media technologies. Building on existing work, researchers should further develop competency-based measures of digital media literacy that encompass the kinds of skills needed to identify and avoid dubious content designed to maximize engagement.

span.quote: Table 2 shows that the age effect remains statistically significant when controlling for ideology and other demographic attributes. The association is also robust to controlling for party, as the various alternative specifications provided in the Supplementary Materials illustrate. In column 2, the coefficient on “Age: over 65” implies that being in the oldest age group was associated with sharing nearly seven times as many articles from fake news domains on Facebook as those in the youngest age group, or about 2.3 times as many as those in the next-oldest age group, holding the effect of ideology, education, and the total number of web links shared constant (e1.9 ≈ 6.69, e1.9−1.079 ≈ 2.27). This association is also found in the specifications using the alternate peer-reviewed measure as a dependent variable in columns 3 and 4, with those over 65 sharing between three and four times as many fake news links as those in the youngest age group.

span.label: the same model applied to hard news sharing gives varied predictors and does not include age
span.term: the same model applied to hard news sharing gives varied predictors and does not include age
span.quote: Last, we show in table S14 that, when we try to explain patterns of hard news sharing behavior using the same approach, the predictors are more varied and do not include age.

span.label: the entire dependent variable is 21 web domains, produced by an engagement ranking, a journalist's inspection and a hard-news classifier
span.term: the entire dependent variable is 21 web domains, produced by an engagement ranking, a journalist's inspection and a hard-news classifier
span.quote: The resulting list contains 21 mostly pro-Trump domains, including well-known purveyors such as abcnews.com.co, the Denver Guardian, and Ending the Fed. In analyses using this list, we counted any article from one of these domains as a fake news share.

span.label: the results are essentially invariant across five different lists of what counts as fake news
span.term: the results are essentially invariant across five different lists of what counts as fake news
span.quote: In addition to these primary measures, we report (below) analyses using three supplementary collections of fake news articles produced after the election. Two lists were also produced by Silverman and his team at BuzzFeed, and the third is a crowdsourced effort headed by Melissa Zimdars of Merrimack College. Our key results are essentially invariant to whatever measure of fake news we use.

span.label: there is no measure of whether respondents knew what they shared was false
span.term: there is no measure of whether respondents knew what they shared was false
span.quote: Figure 2D shows that, if anything, those who share the most content in general were less likely to share articles from fake news–spreading domains to their friends. Thus, it is not the case that what explains fake news sharing is simply that some respondents “will share anything.” These data are consistent with the hypothesis that people who share many links are more familiar with what they are seeing and are able to distinguish fake news from real news. (We note that we have no measure as to whether or not respondents know that what they are sharing is fake news.)

span.label: knowingly false or misleading content created largely for ad revenue - with the authors stating that the term covers a variety of phenomena and that no commonly accepted ground-truth standard exists
span.quote: The term fake news can be used to refer to a variety of different phenomena. Here, we largely adopted the use suggested in of knowingly false or misleading content created largely for the purpose of generating ad revenue. Given the difficulty of establishing a commonly accepted ground-truth standard for what constitutes fake news, our approach was to build on the work of both journalists and academics who worked to document the prevalence of this content over the course of the 2016 election campaign.

span.label: of linked respondents shared no articles from fake news domains at all - the number the title refers to
span.quote: The right panel of Fig. 1 reveals a large spike at 0, with a long tail that goes as far as 50 shares for a single Facebook user, and we see in Table 1 that over 90% of our respondents shared no stories from fake news domains. According to our main measure of fake news content, 8.5% of respondents for whom we have linked Facebook data shared at least one such article to their friends.

span.label: web domains constituting the entire dependent variable, after a journalist's list of 30 was filtered by a hard-news classifier
span.quote: The resulting list contains 21 mostly pro-Trump domains, including well-known purveyors such as abcnews.com.co, the Denver Guardian, and Ending the Fed. In analyses using this list, we counted any article from one of these domains as a fake news share.

span.label: of the 3500 survey respondents agreed to share Facebook profile data; 1191 were successfully linked
span.quote: Of 3500 initial respondents in wave 1, 1331 (38%) agreed to share Facebook profile data with us. The proportion rises (49.1%) when we consider that only 2711 of our respondents said that they use Facebook at all. We were successfully able to link profile data from 1191 of survey respondents, leaving us with approximately 44% of Facebook users in our sample. (See the “Sample details” section for a comparison of sample characteristics on various demographic and behavioral dimensions. Linked respondents were somewhat more knowledgeable and engaged in politics than those who did not share data.)

span.label: the correlation between ideological self-placement and party identification, disclosed and handled by reporting all three specifications
span.quote: In all models, we included either five-point ideological self-placement, three-point party identification, or both. Since these variables were correlated (r = 0.31), we addressed possible multicollinearity via transparency—we provided our main results all three ways.

span.label: quasi-Poisson
span.quote: We aggregated all shares to the individual respondent level so that our dependent variables are counts (i.e., number of fake news stories shared). To account for this feature of the data, as well as the highly skewed distribution of the counts, we primarily used Poisson or quasi-Poisson regressions to model the determinants of Facebook sharing behavior. We conducted dispersion tests on the count data and used quasi-Poisson models if the null hypothesis of no dispersion is rejected. Below, we included negative binomial and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions to show that our results are generally not sensitive to model choice.

span.label: CI
span.quote: Turning to a key demographic characteristic of respondents, a notable finding in Fig. 2B is the clear association between age group and the average number of articles from fake news domains shared on Facebook. Those over 65 shared an average of 0.75 fake news articles (95% CI, 0.515 to 0.977), more than twice as many as those in the second-oldest age group (0.26 articles; 95% CI, 0.206 to 0.314).

span.label: age
span.quote: More puzzling is the independent role of age: Holding constant ideology, party identification, or both, respondents in each age category were more likely to share fake news than respondents in the next-youngest group, and the gap in the rate of fake news sharing between those in our oldest category (over 65) and youngest category is large and notable.
